title: An Enigma of Artificial Reason: Investigating the Production-Evaluation Gap in Large Reasoning Models
claim: Models produce correct reasoning yet fail to evaluate flawed reasoning with valid answers, rationalizing errors, unlike humans who grade nearly as well as they solve.
layout: 2 stacked sections; color-coded solution-to-grading pairs left-to-right, with a gap callout top-right
description: The figure has two parts. Panel (a) at the top shows reasoning production: a blue question box (find the range of f(x)=(3/7)^x) with an arrow to a correct blue answer, and a black callout at top right reading 'Production-Evaluation Gap, LRMs 16–73%, Humans 6%'. Panel (b) shows reasoning evaluation as three color-coded conditions. Green VAVR (valid answer, valid reasoning) and red IAIR (invalid answer) each have a solution box with an arrow to a model grading transcript. Yellow VAIR has four flawed variants (Missing Premises, Shuffled Reasoning, Missing Reasoning, Circular Reasoning) with red text marking flaws. These point to Claude Opus and GPT-5.4 transcripts that notice the flaw, rationalize it away, and give the wrong grade. LRM and human accuracy ranges are shown for each condition.
caption: Overview of our dataset and methodology. We evaluate both large reasoning models (LRMs) and humans on (a) reasoning production as math problem solving (b) reasoning evaluation as math solution grading. We construct the Valid-Answer-Invalid-Reasoning (VAIR) dataset to isolate the reasoning validation task from the confound of answer validity, creating math solutions with trivial reasoning flaws (Missing Premises, ..., Circular Reasoning) but valid answers. Valid-Answer-Valid-Reasoning (VAVR) and Invalid-Answer-Invalid-Reasoning (IAIR) solutions serve as controls. Unlike humans, LRMs exhibit a sharp drop in accuracy (up to 73%) for VAIR evaluation vs. solving problems, demonstrating a large production-evaluation gap (top-right).
abstract: Studies of human reasoning have shown that people are typically stronger at evaluating reasoning than producing it from scratch. In contrast, large reasoning models (LRMs) are trained to excel at producing long chains of reasoning to solve complex problems. How then do LRMs perform at evaluating reasons? We investigate this with the Valid-Answer-Invalid-Reasoning (VAIR) dataset: math problems and solutions with trivial reasoning flaws but valid answers, designed to isolate reasoning evaluation from the confound of reasoning production. Unlike humans, who we find are only 6% worse at grading than solving such problems, we find a substantial production-evaluation gap in LRMs: frontier models score as low as 52% when evaluating VAIR solutions, despite near-perfect solution production. Why this enigma? Through chain-of-thought (CoT) analysis, we find evidence of an answer confirmation bias: LRMs often produce then check for the correct answer instead of carefully verifying each step, fabricating rationalizations even when noticing anomalous reasoning. Linear probes corroborate this, showing that while LRM activations encode some representation of valid reasoning, they fail to robustly represent VAIR solutions as invalid. Causal patching of the final answer's representations causes LRM verdicts and activations to flip at substantial rates, demonstrating that answer validity is a causal factor in models' confirmation biases. These findings indicate an outstanding limitation in dominant approaches to reasoning training, which incentivize LRMs to produce and confirm reasoning towards correct answers, but not to robustly evaluate the underlying reasons
